questions.qtext:
What is output by this program? Assume no errors in executing system calls.

int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
 for (int i = 1; i < 6; ++i) {
 if (fork() == 0) {
 ++i;
 printf("%d", i);
 fflush(stdout);
 } else {
 wait(NULL);
 return 0;
 }
 }
 return 0;
}
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

The loop starts with i = 1. Each time a new child is created, that child bumps its own copy of i up by 1 before printing it, and then the loop itself bumps i up by 1 again before checking the loop condition and forking the next child.

  • Round 1: i is 1 at the fork. The child raises it to 2 and prints 2. The loop then raises it to 3, checks 3 < 6 — true — so it forks again.
  • Round 2: i is 3 at the fork. The child raises it to 4 and prints 4. The loop then raises it to 5, checks 5 < 6 — true — so it forks again.
  • Round 3: i is 5 at the fork. The child raises it to 6 and prints 6. The loop then raises it to 7, checks 7 < 6 — false — loop stops, program ends.

Because each parent waits for its child before doing anything else (and it does nothing else besides exit), there's no overlapping or scrambled output — everything happens in strict sequence, one print at a time, in the order the children are created. ans=246

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

It goes as:

  • Round 1 ($i=1$): Parent forks. The parent hits wait() and stops. The child process steps inside the if, bumps $i$ to 2, and prints 2.

  • Round 2 ($i=3$): That same child loops back around. The loop's ++i kicks $i$ up to 3. It forks a grandchild, then hits wait() and stops. The grandchild steps inside the if, bumps $i$ to 4, and prints 4.

  • Round 3 ($i=5$): That grandchild loops back. The loop's ++i kicks $i$ up to 5. It forks a great-grandchild, then hits wait() and stops. The great-grandchild steps inside the if, bumps $i$ to 6, and prints 6.

After that, the loop condition ($7 < 6$) fails, and the chain of processes collapses back down as they all hit their return statements.

Termination Sequence

Child 3 increments $i$ to $7$. The loop condition $7 < 6$ is false. It reaches the end of main, returns 0, and exits.

Child 2 finishes waiting for Child 3, executes return 0; inside its else block, and exits.

Child 1 finishes waiting for Child 2, executes return 0; inside its else block, and exits.

Parent 1 finishes waiting for Child 1, executes return 0; inside its else block, and exits.

questions.qtext:
You write a UNIX shell, but instead of calling $\texttt{fork()}$ then $\texttt{exec()}$ to launch a new job, you instead insert a subtle difference: the code first calls $\texttt{exec()}$ and then calls $\texttt{fork()}$ like the following:

shell(..) {
 .. ..
 exec(cmd, args);
 fork();
 .. ..
}


Does it work? Enter $0$ if your answer is 'yes', else enter $1$.
questions.solution:
Answer: 1

Source solution 1 (score: 0)
It doesnt work. Shells address space is entirely replaced with the new command $(\texttt{cmd})$, therefore the shell will terminate once $\texttt{cmd}$ is terminated.
Source solution 2 (score: 0)

This ordering breaks the shell fundamentally, because of how exec() works. ans :1

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Think of the exec() command as a complete "brain wipe" for a running process.

When the shell runs exec(), it throws away its own code and completely replaces it with the new program you want to run.

Because the shell's original code is completely wiped out and replaced, it never gets to read the lines of code written below the exec() command.

This means the fork() command sitting right below it is completely erased before the computer ever has a chance to look at it.

Instead of launching a new job in the background and keeping the shell alive, the shell permanently turns into the new program, runs it, and then completely closes down.

Answer: 1

questions.qtext: A compiled program has become corrupted; by means of a one-bit error in the stored program, an unprivileged machine instruction has been replaced by a privileged instruction executable only in kernel mode. When a process is executing this corrupted program, what happens when the erroneous instruction is encountered?

options.text: The processor automatically switches to Kernel Mode so that the instruction can be executed, and then switches back to User Mode following execution of the wayward instruction.
The processor ignores the corrupted instruction, since it cannot execute it in its current User Mode, and proceeds to execute the next instruction following.
The currently running process is aborted, and a different process is dispatched to the processor.
The system crashes and must be rebooted.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 0)
C is correct because when operating in User mode, a kernel-mode instruction is treated as an illegal instruction
Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Option C is correct because the process is shut down immediately. When a normal program tries to run a restricted kernel command, the CPU hardware catches it, stops the program, and switches to another process.

Option A is incorrect because the CPU will never let a regular program automatically switch itself to kernel mode. If it did, security would be completely broken.

Option B is incorrect because the CPU cannot just skip or ignore a bad instruction. It must flag the error immediately.

Option D is incorrect because the computer does not crash or need a reboot. The operating system blocks the bad program and keeps the rest of the computer running safely.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

  • The Hardware Trap: Modern processors use dual-mode operation (User Mode and Kernel Mode) to protect the system. If a process running in User Mode attempts to execute a privileged instruction, the CPU hardware catches this and generates an exception (specifically, a trap or fault) to the Operating System.

  • The OS Response (Option C): The OS handles this exception. Because a user program attempted an illegal, privileged action, the OS protects the system by terminating (aborting) the offending process. It then invokes the scheduler to dispatch a different process to the processor.

  • Why the others are incorrect:

    • A is incorrect: If processors automatically switched to Kernel Mode for any privileged instruction, there would be no security; any user program could take full control of the machine.

    • B is incorrect: Processors do not silently ignore illegal instructions, as doing so would cause the program to behave unpredictably and corrupt data.

    • D is incorrect: The entire purpose of protecting privileged instructions is to prevent user-level errors from crashing the whole system. Only the corrupted process is killed; the OS remains stable.

options.text: When a user-level process wishes to call a function inside the kernel, it directly jumps to the desired function.
A system call can only be called in kernel mode.
The OS may manipulate the contents of a Memory Management Unit.
Threads that are part of the same process share the same Program Counter.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, D

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

answer is A,B,D

Source solution 2 (score: 0)
  • Option A is false because a user-level process cannot directly jump to a function inside the kernel.

A direct jump instruction to kernel space would violate security , so the process must instead trigger a trap or software interrupt to let the kernel safely handle the switch.

  • Option B is false because a system call is explicitly invoked from user mode by an unprivileged program when it needs to request services from the kernel.

If a program were already running in kernel mode, it would execute kernel functions directly instead of making a system call wrapper invitation.

  • Option C is true because the operating system kernel is completely responsible for configuring and modifying page tables and translation lookaside buffers inside the MMU

This allows the OS to handle memory isolation and address translations securely.

  • Option D is false because each individual thread inside the same process must track its own independent execution flow.

Every thread contains its own unique program counter and set of registers so it can execute different parts of the code at the same time.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

  • A. FALSE — A user process cannot directly jump (jmp / call) to kernel memory address locations because user mode lacks privilege to execute arbitrary kernel memory. Instead, it must trigger a system call via a software interrupt or a dedicated trap instruction (like syscall or sysenter), passing the request through a well-defined kernel entry point (trap table).

  • B. FALSE — System calls are initiated by user-level processes executing in user mode to request services from the OS kernel. (Executing the system call instruction transitions the processor from user mode into kernel mode).

  • C. TRUE — The OS manages memory page tables, TLBs, and base/bound registers, directly manipulating the MMU settings during context switches and page fault handling.

  • D. FALSE — Each thread has its own independent execution flow, which means every thread maintains its own Program Counter (PC), stack, and register set, even though they share the process's overall address space.

options.text: A buggy thread may be able to overwrite variables belonging to another thread of the same process.
On a context switch across threads of the same process, the general-purpose registers must be saved and restored.
Threads in the same process share the same $\text{SP}$ (Stack Pointer).
User processes reference their address space with physical addresses.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Option A is true because threads share the same global memory space, allowing a faulty thread to overwrite memory regions used by other threads in the same process.

Option B is true because saving and restoring general-purpose registers is absolutely necessary to preserve the independent CPU state of each thread during a context switch.

Option C is false because each thread possesses its own private stack and separate stack pointer to execute its functions independently without interfering with other threads.

Option D is false because user processes strictly reference their address space using virtual addresses, relying completely on hardware translation to map them to real physical addresses.

Therefore, the false options are C and D.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

  • A. TRUE — Threads within the same process share the same global address space (heap, data segment, global variables). Because there is no memory isolation between threads of a single process, a buggy thread (e.g., via a wild pointer or stack overflow) can easily overwrite memory used by another thread.

  • B. TRUE — When switching execution from one thread to another, the processor's general-purpose registers (including the stack pointer and program counter) contain computation state specific to the outgoing thread. These registers must be saved to the thread control block (TCB) and restored from the incoming thread's TCB.

  • C. FALSE — Each thread must maintain its own call stack to manage function calls, local variables, and return addresses independently. Therefore, every thread has its own Stack Pointer (SP).

  • D. FALSE — User processes operate using virtual addresses generated by the CPU. The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates these virtual addresses into physical addresses. User processes do not have direct access to physical address space for memory protection and virtualization reasons.

questions.qtext:
Consider the following code segment. What is the total number of processes, including the initial process?

#include<stdlib.h>
#include<stdio.h>
#include<unistd.h>
int main() {
 for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
 if (fork()) {
 fork();
 }
 else {
 fork();
 fork();
 }
 }
 return 0;
}
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 3)
There are total $6^{10}$ processes. In each loop, there are $4$ $\texttt{fork()}$ operations. The first $\texttt{fork()}$ creates one child $(1)$. The second $\texttt{fork()}$ create one child, the third fork create $1$ child, and the forth $\texttt{fork()}$ create $2$ children. So after one loop there are $6$ processes from the initial $1$ process. And since there are $10$ loops, after this program totally there are $6^{10}$ processes.
Source solution 2 (score: 0)
After the first iteration, 1 process becomes 6 processes. Since all 6 processes continue to execute the loop, each subsequent iteration again multiplies the current number of processes by 6.Option C is correct.

options.text: The $\texttt{fork()}$ system call clones the calling process and overlays a new file image on the child process.
Threads from different processes can share the same address space.
Accessing a threads stack from a different thread raises a segmentation fault.
The child process may run concurrently with the parent process.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Option A is false because fork only duplicates the current process structure, while loading a new file image requires a separate exec system call.

Option B is false because different processes possess completely isolated address spaces, meaning their respective threads cannot share memory space.

Option C is false because all threads within the same process share a single address space, so accessing another thread's stack will not trigger a segmentation fault

Option D is true because once the child process is created, the operating system can schedule both the parent and child to run concurrently.

Therefore, the false options are A, B, and C.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

  • A. FALSE

    • fork() creates an exact duplicate (clone) of the calling process. Overlaying a new executable binary/file image onto a process is performed by the exec() family of system calls, not fork().

  • B. FALSE

    • Each process operates within its own isolated virtual address space. Threads belonging to different processes do not share an address space; only threads belonging to the same process share their memory address space.

  • C. FALSE

    • Since all threads in the same process share the same address space, memory protection operates at the process level, not the individual thread stack level. If Thread A accesses an address located on Thread B's stack (e.g., via a shared pointer), the CPU/OS will allow it without raising a segmentation fault.

  • D. TRUE

    • After a call to fork(), both the parent and the child processes run concurrently unless the parent explicitly calls wait() to suspend execution until the child finishes.

options.text: The only reason to isolate the kernel from users is security.
A system call is an interrupt.
System calls can be interrupted.
$\texttt{strcmp()}$ is a system call.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Option A: False because Other reasons include:

  • Protecting the operating system from buggy user programs.
  • Ensuring system stability and reliability.
  • Preventing accidental corruption of kernel memory.
  • Enforcing privilege separation
Option B: False bcz

A system call is not an interrupt. It is a software-generated trap/exception that transfers control from user mode to kernel mode.Interrupt is generated by hardware like keyboard,mouse,timer

Option C : True

Option D : False bcz it compares to strings

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Option A is false because security is not the sole reason for kernel isolation.

Option B is false because system calls are traps rather than asynchronous hardware interrupts.

Option C is true because kernel execution can be paused by interrupts.

Option D is false because strcmp is a basic user-level library function.

Therefore, the false options are A, B, and D.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

  • A. "The only reason to isolate the kernel from users is security." — FALSE

    • While security (preventing malicious programs from gaining unauthorized access) is a key reason, it is not the only reason. Isolation also ensures reliability and fault containment (preventing a buggy user application from crashing the entire operating system) and provides clean hardware abstraction.

  • B. "A system call is an interrupt." — FALSE

    • Strictly speaking, an interrupt is an asynchronous hardware signal generated by external devices (e.g., keyboard, network card, timer). A system call is a synchronous software request generated by a running program using a trap or system call instruction (syscall/sysenter). While sometimes loosely termed a "software interrupt," they are conceptually distinct mechanisms.

  • C. "System calls can be interrupted." — TRUE

    • When CPU is executing code inside a system call in kernel mode, hardware interrupts (such as a timer interrupt or disk I/O completion interrupt) can still occur and temporarily preempt the kernel execution (unless interrupts are explicitly masked/disabled in a critical section).

  • D. strcmp() is a system call. — FALSE

    • strcmp() is a standard C library function (<string.h>). It performs simple character-by-character string comparison in user space and does not require kernel intervention or system calls.

questions.qtext:
Consider the following two programs. $\texttt{waitpid()}$ makes a parent process wait for a specific child process (given by $\text{PID}$) to finish execution.

// Program A
int x = 5;
int main() {
 int pid = fork();
 if (pid == 0) {
 x = 2;
 execv("B", "2");
 }
 else {
 waitpid(pid);
 printf("%d", x);
 }
}

// Program B
int x = 0;
int main(int argv, char **argc) {
 int pid = fork();
 if (pid == 0) {
 execv("B", "1");
 }
 else {
 waitpid(pid);
 printf("%d", x);
 }
 return 1;
}


Which of the following is the output when Program $\text{A}$ is executed?

options.text: No output is produced

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

When Program A starts executing, a global variable x is initialized to 5.

The main function calls fork, which clones the process into a parent process and a child process.

For the parent process, fork returns the child's PID, moving execution directly into the else block.

Inside the else block, the parent hits waitpid(pid), forcing it to block and wait until that specific child process fully finishes execution.

Meanwhile, the child process enters the if block because its pid value is 0.

The child updates its own local copy of x to 2, which does not affect the parent's copy of x due to separate process address spaces.

The child then calls execv("B", "2"), which completely overwrites the child process image with the executable Program B.

Program B starts executing from its own main function, which initializes its own global variable x to 0.

Inside Program B, fork is called again, splitting this child process into a nested sub-parent and a nested sub-child.

The nested sub-child enters the if block and calls execv("B", "1"), loading a new instance of Program B that forks yet again.

This creates an infinite chain of forks and exec calls because the child branch of Program B always invokes execv("B", "1"), meaning the execution path inside the child processes never terminates.

Because this sequence of child processes continues to fork infinitely without ever exiting, the original child process of Program A never terminates.

Since the original child never terminates, the parent process of Program A remains blocked inside the waitpid(pid) system call.

As a result, the parent process never proceeds to the next line to execute printf("%d", x).

Because the parent is stuck indefinitely and the child processes only perform forks and execs without any print statements, no output is ever written to the console.

Therefore, option D is the correct choice..

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Correct answer: D. No output is produced

Here's why:

Program A

After fork():

  • The parent calls waitpid(pid), so it waits for the child.
  • The child executes Program B using execv().
Program B

x is initialized to 0.

Then B does another fork():

  • The child again executes Program B.
  • The parent waits for that child before printing x.

This repeats indefinitely:

B→B→B→⋯

Since every parent waits for its child, none of them ever reaches the printf().

Therefore:

D. No output is produced​
